newsitem.title: USA: U.S. proposes ban on some livestock feed to prevent BSE.
newsitem.headline: U.S. proposes ban on some livestock feed to prevent BSE.

text.p: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration on Thursday proposed to ban the practice of feeding reprocessed animal tissue to other animals in a move to protect livestock from the dreaded mad cow disease and a possible spread of the fatal disease to humans.
The FDA proposed to prohibit using tissues from ruminants -- cud-chewing animals such as cows, sheep and goats -- in the manufacture of feed intended for cattle and other ruminants.

The proposed regulation was taken to protect animals from transmissable degenerative neurological diseases -- among these BSE (bovine spongiform encephalopathy), or mad cow disease -- and to minimise any risk that such diseases could be transmitted from animals to humans.
"This is a precautionary measure -- there have been no reported cases of BSE in this country," said Secretary of Health and Human Services Donna Shalala of the FDA action.

FDA's proposed regulation would prohibit the use of nearly all potential sources of ruminant, and also mink protein, in feed for cattle and other ruminants. Chicken and hog feed, along with pet food, will not be affected by the new rule.
The proposal is now open to 45 days of public comment. An FDA official said the agency wants to move quickly on adopting a final rule.
"We expect to be able to move fairly quickly," said Lawrence Bachorik. "We expect a final rule in a matter of months ... this is a priority."

The feeding of recycled animal protein back to animals has long been a common practice in the feed industry. Almost 4 billion pounds of animals and animal parts that are not used in packing go into feed every year, said an industry source.
Renderers process the unnused animal parts, separate the fat from the protein, grind the protein up into a flaky substance and mix it with other feed ingredients.

The safety of feeding animal protein was questioned after the first case of BSE was reported in the United Kingdom in 1986. Evidence gathered in the UK suggests an association between the BSE outbreak there and the feeding to cattle of protein from sheep infected with scrapie, another transmissable spongiform encephalopathies, or TSE.

Over the next 10 years, about 165,000 head of cattle in over 33,000 herds were diagnosed with BSE in the United Kingdom. The disease has also been confirmed in domestic cattle in Ireland, France, Portugal, Oman and Switzerland.

Recently, scientists have linked BSE to a new variant form of Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease reported in the UK, a fatal degenerative neurological disorder affecting humans. The newly identified CJD, which leaves spongelike holes in the brain, has killed 10 people in Britain.
While some U.S. animal feed industry officials said the FDA action is unnecessary because BSE has never been detected in the United States, the cattle industry welcomed the move.
"We applaud the government for its continued efforts to to prevent this," said Alisa Harrison of the National Cattlemen's Beef Association.

Harrison said the rule is likely to have little effect on the price of livestock production, since beef and dairy producers have already cut back sharply on their use of animal protein in feed rations.
